definition: Epistolary means carried on through or consisting of letters.
task: Write one sentence of your own using the word epistolary. Make the sentence show what the word means -- a reader who did not know epistolary should be able to work it out from your sentence.
avoid_verbatim: The playwright built the second act as an epistolary duet: two soldiers reading aloud the letters they exchanged across enemy lines.
A spoken exchange commits nothing to paper, stopping far short of an epistolary one, which lives entirely in letters.
Written covers anything set down on paper, but it stops short of epistolary, which says the exchange itself was conducted through letters, mailed and answered.

Postal describes the mail system that moves the letters — stamps, carriers, sorting offices. Epistolary describes what the letters add up to: a friendship, feud, or novel carried on through them. A postal strike is about delivery; an epistolary novel is about letters doing the telling.

Handwritten says only that a pen, not a keyboard, produced the words — a grocery list qualifies. Epistolary is about form, not penmanship: an exchange conducted through letters, sent and answered. A typed love letter is epistolary but not handwritten.

Textual describes words as text on a page — textual evidence, a textual error — and belongs to editing and analysis. Epistolary names a form instead: an exchange carried on through letters. A scholar's textual notes may study an epistolary novel; the notes concern wording, the novel is made of letters.

Epistolary means carried on through or consisting of letters.

Their courtship was entirely epistolary: he was posted to a lighthouse and she taught in the capital, so for three years everything — jokes, quarrels, the proposal itself — traveled by the weekly mail boat.

Epistolary is the exact word for something carried on through letters, from a friendship to a novel's whole structure; 'written' is too broad, and 'postal' describes the mail system rather than the relationship or the form.
Epistolary is a book-review and history-seminar word.
Use it for novels told in letters and for friendships, feuds, or courtships conducted by mail; for anything less specific, 'written' or 'by mail' is plainer and usually better.

In 1861 two botanists, one in Edinburgh and one in Bombay, began comparing notes on the ferns each was finding.
They never met, yet over thirty years they built a complete theory of spore dispersal together, one mailed packet at a time.

When their heirs published the correspondence in 1904, reviewers marveled that the science was inseparable from its epistolary form: every hypothesis was proposed in one letter and tested by the next.
A modern editor calls the volume an experiment conducted by envelope, and the description has stuck.
Readers today can watch two careful minds change each other in slow motion, a record no laboratory notebook could have preserved.
